summary: Specifies how NAT devices should behave when handling ICMP, making them more predictable and compatible with the many applications whose traffic passes through them. It is a companion to other documents on NAT behavior requirements and is a best current practice.

eli5.summary: A mailroom that changes return addresses must also handle error notes correctly. This note lays out how those address-changing boxes should treat network error messages.

questions: how should a nat handle icmp
how long should a nat keep icmp query mappings
why does nat need to translate icmp errors
subtitle: How a NAT should treat ICMP pings, traceroutes and error messages so applications keep working through it.

tldr.problem: NAT devices handle ICMP in widely differing ways, which makes them unpredictable and breaks applications such as ping, traceroute and path MTU discovery.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets eleven numbered requirements (REQ-1 to REQ-11) covering ICMP queries, ICMP error translation, hairpinning, rejected flows and which ICMP messages a NAT must support.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice for IPv4 traditional NATs and is updated by RFC 7857. It is a companion to the TCP and UDP NAT requirements documents.

today: RFC 5508 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 148) and has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 7857. Read the two together.

sections.title: Why NATs Need ICMP Rules
sections.content:
RFC 5508 defines how a Network Address Translator (NAT) should behave with the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP). Its goal is to reduce the unpredictability and brittleness that NATs introduce. It is a companion to the NAT requirements for UDP (RFC 4787) and TCP (RFC 5382).

The rules apply to traditional NATs as described in RFC 3022: Basic NAT and the Network Address Port Translator (NAPT), which lets several private hosts share one public IP address. The text covers IPv4 only. Firewall functionality and application behavior are out of scope.

Local policy can override many of the rules. An administrator may block ICMP errors or ICMP-query applications entirely, so several requirements begin with the condition that local policy permits.
sections.eli5: Address-swapping boxes handle error notes in many different ways, so things break. This note says what they should all do.

sections.title: Query, Error and Other ICMP Messages
sections.content:
The RFC splits ICMP into three classes, because each class is identified differently for NAT mapping.

  • ICMP Query messages carry an Identifier field (the Query Id). The Query Id plays the role that a port plays for TCP and UDP.
  • ICMP Error messages embed the original datagram that triggered the error, called the embedded packet. They have no Query Id.
  • Non-QueryError messages fit neither group, such as Router Discovery messages, which have no Identifier field.

A NAT session is the association between a session seen in the private realm and the same session seen in the public realm. Here it is limited to TCP, UDP and ICMP sessions.
sections.eli5: Some notes are questions with a ticket number, some are complaints that quote the original letter, and a few are neither. The box has to treat each kind its own way.

sections.title: Handling ICMP Queries
sections.content:
REQ-1: unless local policy says otherwise, a NAT MUST permit ICMP Queries, and their responses, started by a private host toward external hosts. A NAPT device also rewrites the Query Id and the ICMP checksum. The mapping of Query Ids SHOULD be external-host independent: if host A reuses Query Id X toward another external host, the NAT SHOULD reuse the same external Query Id. This is only a SHOULD because ping and traceroute do not need it, while future applications might.

REQ-2: an ICMP Query session timer MUST NOT expire in less than 60 seconds, and it is RECOMMENDED to be configurable. The RFC reasons from the TCP Maximum Segment Lifetime of 120 seconds, which would give a maximum round trip of 240 seconds, and notes that ping and traceroute normally finish a round trip in under 10 seconds. A long timeout ties up NAT resources, a short one frees them too early, and 60 seconds is the stated balance.
sections.eli5: If you send a question out, the box must remember who asked for at least a minute, so the answer finds its way back to you.

sections.title: Forwarding ICMP Errors
sections.content:
Many applications use ICMP errors to shorten their timeouts, and some do not work without them. The NAT finds the right session by looking inside the embedded packet.

Validation (REQ-3). The NAT SHOULD silently drop an error whose ICMP checksum is invalid, and one whose embedded IP checksum is invalid. If the embedded packet has IP options, the NAT MUST skip past them to find the transport header. The NAT SHOULD NOT check the embedded transport checksum, because the error often holds only part of the transport segment and end hosts are better placed to judge it. If ICMP extensions are present, the NAT MUST leave out the zero padding and extensions when it evaluates that checksum.

Translation (REQ-4 and REQ-5). With no active mapping for the embedded packet, the NAT SHOULD silently drop the error. Otherwise it MUST restore the embedded IP and transport headers to their original form and leave the ICMP type and code unchanged. For an error from the external realm it then sets the outer destination address to the translated source of the embedded packet. For an error from the private realm, a Basic NAT with a mapping for the sender uses that public address as the outer source. In all other cases the NAT uses its own public address.

Session state (REQ-6). While processing an error about an ICMP Query or response, the NAT MUST NOT refresh or delete the related NAT session. This stops a spoofed error from changing the session.
sections.eli5: When a complaint note arrives, the box reads the quoted letter inside, works out who it was really for, fixes the addresses, and passes it on. It ignores notes it cannot match.

sections.title: Hairpinning and Rejected Flows
sections.content:
Hairpinning (REQ-7). Hairpinning means a private host reaching another private host through the NAT's public address. Basic NAT devices MUST support hairpinned ICMP Query sessions. All NAT devices, Basic NAT and NAPT, MUST support hairpinned ICMP errors, and MUST set the outer destination address to the source address of the embedded packet after translation.

Rejected flows (REQ-8). When a NAT cannot set up a session for a new flow because of resource limits or administrative restrictions, it SHOULD send ICMP destination unreachable with code 13 (Communication administratively prohibited) and drop the original packet. The RFC says this is mainly for future use. It strongly discourages designs that never reject and instead steal resources from existing sessions.
sections.eli5: If two kids in the same house send notes to each other through the front-door mailbox, the box must still deliver them. And if it is too busy, it should say so politely instead of quietly throwing away someone else's mail.

sections.title: Conformance to the Router Rules
sections.content:
NATs should treat ICMP like routers do under RFC 1812, except where that RFC is out of date. REQ-9 lets a NAT have a policy control that stops ICMP messages being generated toward certain interfaces, and such a policy overrides REQ-10.

REQ-10 sorts ICMP messages by support level. A NAT MUST honor the DF bit and, if it cannot forward without fragmenting, MUST send a 'Packet Too Big' message (type 3, code 4) with the next-hop MTU. It MUST also forward such messages it receives, and MUST generate Time Exceeded when TTL expires, which keeps traceroute working. Address Mask, Parameter Problem and Router Advertisement support is not required, since the RFC calls them rarely used where IPv4 NATs run. A NAT SHOULD copy the diffserv class of the triggering packet into ICMP messages it generates.

REQ-11 says a NAT MAY drop or handle Non-QueryError messages, and the RFC gives no further guidance.
sections.eli5: The box should behave like a normal post office on delivery trouble notes, but it can skip a few old, rarely used kinds.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it introduces no new security concerns and that its rules mitigate some known ICMP problems. Dropping errors with bad checksums or with no matching mapping keeps bogus ICMP errors from reaching end hosts, although checksum checks alone do not protect hosts from attacks. REQ-6 prevents a forged error from tearing down a session.

Some administrators may decide not to send the REQ-8 error, since it could tell an attacker that an attack worked, so that choice is left to the administrator. The RFC also notes that blocking ICMP at network boundaries breaks path MTU discovery, ping and traceroute, and calls such blocking NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: The box throws away fake or garbled notes and will not let a fake note make it forget a real conversation.
